The ImPossible Tour

By: Laura Byrne | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Grant Lottering has faced impossible odds on the bicycle - but he continues to push the boundaries of endurance.

Unique Selling Point:
IN 2013 former professional cyclist Grant Lottering almost died on the side of the road in Italy after a dramatic crash during preparation for the world champs. He was told he would never get on a bike again but he swore from his hospital bed to complete the race in which he had crashed - the next year, he did. Since then, he has completed one solo ultra-endurance feat after another and proved the strength of the human spirit.

Summary:
Grant Lottering was a professional cyclist who in July 2013 was training for the world champs in a 140km preparation race in Trento, Italy. Rounding a corner in the rain at 60km/h he crashed into a rock embankment, collapsing his lungs and thorax, crushing his shoulder, fracturing 12 ribs, his spine, femur, scapula, clavicle, and sternum, rupturing arteries…His heart had stopped beating by the time the medical team arrived. He was told he was lucky to be alive and would never ride a bike again.

But even while he was still in hospital, he swore he would return the next year to complete the race in which he had crashed and one year later, after six surgeries and 83 rehabilitation sessions, he completed the ride 170km La Marmotte through the Alps, then the Charly Gaul – the race in which he almost died. Over the following four years he has tackled one endurance feat after another, riding hundreds of kilometres through the Alps under conditions that have ranged from tricky to treacherous. He has not always succeeded - in 2017 he was forced to give up due to freezing temperatures and howling wind - but he has proved the ability of the human spirit to triumph over impossible odds.

Further information:
In 2015, Lottering did the second Im’Possible tour: he became the first South African to complete a solo, non-stop, 414km ultra-endurance ride through the French Alps in 24 hours. He cycled over eight alpine mountains and climbed 1 000m higher than Mount Everest in one day. He still had two metal pins in his right leg and hip, as well as a still-fractured right clavicle held in place with plates and screws.

In 2016, Lottering completed his 3rd Im'possible tour: 962km in 46 hours of continuous riding, climbing 20,000m over 20 Alpine mountains and riding throughout the night twice.

On 2 July 2017, Grant Lottering set out to tackle his 4th Im’possible Tour: 40 mountains, climbing 44 700m, over a distance of 1800km, in under 96 hours, non-stop. But below zero temperatures and a gale-force wind forced him to submit and he gave up after covering 406km and 9 mountains, a total elevation gain of 11 400m.

In September 2018 he returned for his final tour: a gruelling traverse of the entire Pyrenees, from the Col d’Aubisque in the Western Pyrenees to the ski station of Les Saisies in the Northern Alps. He arrived at Les Saisies at 13:34 on 4 September, 72 hours and 34 minutes after setting out, having faced challenges from road closures forcing detours to getting lost in the middle of the night and cycling up the wrong mountains before having to make a U-turn, to rain that made the descents treacherous, dangerous and slow. Throughout the 72 hour ordeal, Lottering never slept, but ‘napped’ in the support car, totalling only three hours and 40 minutes of sleep in three days.

To date, Lottering’s annual Im’possible Tours have raised over R2 million for this worthy organisation that fosters a love for sport in disadvantaged communities. He now works as a motivational speaker, using his story to inspire others to triumph against the odds.

Press Release:


IN 2013 former professional cyclist Grant Lottering almost died on the side of the road in Italy after a dramatic crash during preparation for the world champs. He was told he would never get on a bike again but he swore from his hospital bed to complete the race in which he had crashed - the next year, he did. Since then, he has completed one solo ultra-endurance feat after another and proved the strength of the human spirit.

Script:


VO1: Midnight in the Alps. It’s remote, bitterly cold. Up the steep slope comes a lone figure.
Grant Lottering’s Im’Possible Tour is a triumph against human limitations. His journey started in these very mountains, five years ago.
UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: I trained for an entire year really hard. So I arrived there probably the best shape of my life.
VO2: A lifelong love of the sport led former professional cyclist Grant to the starting line of the Charly Gaul, a gruelling 140km race in Italy, on 21 July 2013.
LINK 1: Grant had completed dozens of tough races around the world, but little did he know that that day, he would face his biggest challenge yet.
UPSOUND: Grant: I was racing to win. The next minute I was desperately trying to live. We came round this corner, I was too wide, there was water running down the side and next thing there’s this rock in front of me. I just remember lying there screaming, trying to breathe, vomiting blood. Immediately I knew I’ve got a serious problem.
VO3: The impact crushed Grant’s right shoulder, broke two vertebrae, his sternum, leg and 12 ribs. It ruptured arteries, caused internal bleeding, and collapsed his lungs and thorax. By the time the medical team arrived, his heart had stopped.
UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: When you can’t breathe you start to hear your heart beat in your ears and that’s all I could hear. And then I lost my sight. It was actually a peaceful moment that I had in the midst of that absolute chaos and I woke up in ICU the next day.
UPSOUND: Glenn Lottering: I was horrified. All you could see was pipes, bandages, it was hectic.
VO4: Grant’s brother Glenn drove from his home in the Netherlands to Italy, where Grant spent days in intensive care.
UPSOUND: Glenn Lottering: He was living for small things at that time, getting the pipes out, being able to go to the bathroom on his own.
VO5: Doctors told Grant he would never ride again. But even from his hospital bed, he resolved to return to the Charly Gaul the very next year.
UPSOUND: Glenn Lottering: Grant just said to me, I don’t believe them, I’m going to prove them wrong.
LINK 2: After 21 days in hospital, Grant was flown home. Here at MediClinic Sandton, he started his long journey back to health.
UPSOUND: Derek Watts: Phillip when Grant returned from Italy, what sort of state was he in?
Dr Phillip Webster: He was very thin, he weighed 58kg. He was mostly in a wheelchair and crutches.
VO6: Dr Phillip Webster reconstructed Grant’s shattered shoulder.
UPSOUND: Dr Webster: He had what we call a floating shoulder. So all of the attachment of the shoulder to the rest of the body was gone.
VO7: Grant underwent five surgeries in four months and began treatment with physiotherapist Marlinde de Vries.
UPSOUND: Derek Watts: Was the treatment then just to get him back on the road or to be a racing snake?
Marlinde de Vries: No, we didn’t even consider getting him back onto a bike, I just wanted him to get him to use his arm, to lift it up, to put on a t-shirt, to make himself a cup of coffee, to drive to work.
UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: To be honest with you, there was nobody that agreed with what I was planning, simply because of the immense risk I took.
UPSOUND: Marlinde de Vries: I remember thinking I’d better send him back to the surgeon because I didn’t want to be the one to tell him that he wasn’t going to ride again.
UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: I literally had to force myself to not look at what I see and what everyone tells me, but to focus on what I believe in.
UPSOUND: Dr Webster: I said I think it’s far too early to do it. And the next time he spoke to me was when he came back and said he’d done it.
VO8: Eleven months after his accident, Grant returned to Italy and completed the Charly Gaul.
UPSOUND: Glenn Lottering: The shoulder was so weak he couldn’t hold the handlebar. He was in so much pain.
UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: It was still the hardest most painful ride I’ve ever done in my life, but also the most significant and most rewarding.
VO9: The triumph whetted Grant’s appetite for the impossible.
UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: I’ve done this with half a body literally. So I’m going to come back next year and I said to him I want to double.
VO10: So the Im’Possible Tour was born, an annual solo ultra-endurance challenge. Driven by his brush with death, Grant invested his mission with a social purpose.
UPSOUND: Morne du Plessis: Grant is quite obviously one of the bravest, determined people you would ever meet. He epitomises everything our organisation stands for.
VO11: Morne du Plessis is chairperson of the Laureus Sport for Good Foundation which uses sports to drive social change. As an ambassador, Grant raises funds and awareness for its 26 local programmes.
UPSOUND: Morne du Plessis: The funding is just one of the goals. The life lessons, the motivation, the inspiration that comes with this is as important.
UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: I’m not on my own time anymore. This is a second chance at life I’ve been given. So I don’t want a day to go by that I waste it.
LINK 3: Year after year, Grant returned to the mountains that almost took his life, pushing himself to the limits of endurance.
VO12: In 2015, he was the first South African to complete a solo, non-stop, 420km ride through the French Alps in under 24 hours, climbing 10 000m.
In 2016, he rode 962km in 46 hours, climbing 20,000m.
UPSOUND: Glenn Lottering: Some of the routes, your cellphone doesn’t work, there’s no GPS, it’s tiny little roads.
UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: I started hallucinating at times. I’d see hands in the bushes or a dog chasing me.
Derek Watts: The battle’s with yourself really.
Grant Lottering: Oh yeah. I know every demon [laughs]
VO13: Following a cancer scare and more surgery, Grant set out in 2017 hoping to smash his own records.
UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: I was going to ride 4 days, 1800km.
UPSOUND: Glenn Lottering: What we weren’t prepared for was the temperatures that hit us that evening. The middle of the summer and suddenly we’re at minus 5, minus 10 degrees Celsius.
UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: And by the next morning, I had ridden 400km, 20 hours and I already had hypothermia.
VO14: Forced to give up, it was with even greater determination that Grant returned to those unforgiving mountains this year.
UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: This is where I started, down in the Pyrenees near Spain.
VO15: His route traversed the Pyrenees and the Alps, a total of 961km and over 21 000m of climbing in an ordeal lasting more than 72 hours.
UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: Finished about an hour’s drive south of Geneva, Les Saisies. 23 mountains. Nineteen of the mountains I rode was in the Tour de France this year.
UPSOUND: Glenn Lottering: Imagine you take 23 days of the Tour de France, or maybe let’s say 18, and you squeeze that into 2, 3 days.
VO16: Grant faced road closures, getting lost in the middle of the night and rain that made the roads treacherous. He totalled less than 4 hours’ sleep.
UPSOUND: Glenn Lottering: You come around a corner, he’s doing 80km an hour on a downhill and the sheep are lying in the road. When you get to the bottom you say a little prayer and you move on.
VO17: It was a triumph of teamwork – and marked R2 million raised for Laureus.
LINK 4: Well it’s Grant’s last European tour for now – but he has big plans to take on the South African landscape.
UPSOUND: Grant: I want to ride across this country, five provinces. It’s going to be even harder than what I did this year.
Derek Watts: Have you ever thought of table tennis? Very good sport.
UPSOUND: Morne du Plessis: His story is about dedication and determination and getting up again. Sport with meaning.
UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: Like anything in life, if you really put your mind to it and you commit and you persevere, you can accomplish some incredible things.

PROMO 1: 10 SECONDS
VO: After a near-fatal crash five years ago, Grant Lottering was told he’d never cycle again. But he turned defeat into triumph as an ultra-endurance athlete.

PROMO 2: 15 SECONDS
UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: I was racing to win. The next minute I was desperately trying to live.
VO: Cyclist Grant Lottering survived a devastating crash five years ago. Now his annual Im’Possible tour tests the limits of human endurance.

PROMO 3: 15 SECONDS
VO: After a near-fatal accident, ultra-endurance cyclist Grant Lottering is testing the strength of the human spirit.
UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: I’m not on my own time anymore. This is a second chance at life I’ve been given. So I don’t want a day to go by that I waste it.

PROMO 4: 30 SECONDS
UPSOUND Grant Lottering: I just remember lying there screaming, trying to breathe, vomiting blood. Immediately I knew I’ve got a serious problem.
VO: A cycling accident almost killed him five years ago, but Grant Lottering refused to accept defeat. Now his Im’Possible tour tests the limits of human endurance.
UPSOUND: Morne du Plessis: His story is about dedication and determination and getting up again. port with meaning.
UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: I’m not on my own time anymore.

LINK 1: Grant had completed dozens of tough races around the world, but little did he know that that day, he would face his biggest challenge yet. UPSOUND: Grant: I was racing to win. The next minute I was desperately trying to live. We came round this corner, I was too wide, there was water running down the side and next thing there’s this rock in front of me. I just remember lying there screaming, trying to breathe, vomiting blood. Immediately I knew I’ve got a serious problem. VO3: The impact crushed Grant’s right shoulder, broke two vertebrae, his sternum, leg and 12 ribs. It ruptured arteries, caused internal bleeding, and collapsed his lungs and thorax. By the time the medical team arrived, his heart had stopped. UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: When you can’t breathe you start to hear your heart beat in your ears and that’s all I could hear. And then I lost my sight. It was actually a peaceful moment that I had in the midst of that absolute chaos and I woke up in ICU the next day. UPSOUND: Glenn Lottering: I was horrified. All you could see was pipes, bandages, it was hectic. VO4: Grant’s brother Glenn drove from his home in the Netherlands to Italy, where Grant spent days in intensive care. UPSOUND: Glenn Lottering: He was living for small things at that time, getting the pipes out, being able to go to the bathroom on his own. VO5: Doctors told Grant he would never ride again. But even from his hospital bed, he resolved to return to the Charly Gaul the very next year. UPSOUND: Glenn Lottering: Grant just said to me, I don’t believe them, I’m going to prove them wrong. LINK 2: After 21 days in hospital, Grant was flown home. Here at MediClinic Sandton, he started his long journey back to health. UPSOUND: Derek Watts: Phillip when Grant returned from Italy, what sort of state was he in? Dr Phillip Webster: He was very thin, he weighed 58kg. He was mostly in a wheelchair and crutches. VO6: Dr Phillip Webster reconstructed Grant’s shattered shoulder. UPSOUND: Dr Webster: He had what we call a floating shoulder. So all of the attachment of the shoulder to the rest of the body was gone. VO7: Grant underwent five surgeries in four months and began treatment with physiotherapist Marlinde de Vries. UPSOUND: Derek Watts: Was the treatment then just to get him back on the road or to be a racing snake? Marlinde de Vries: No, we didn’t even consider getting him back onto a bike, I just wanted him to get him to use his arm, to lift it up, to put on a t-shirt, to make himself a cup of coffee, to drive to work. UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: To be honest with you, there was nobody that agreed with what I was planning, simply because of the immense risk I took. UPSOUND: Marlinde de Vries: I remember thinking I’d better send him back to the surgeon because I didn’t want to be the one to tell him that he wasn’t going to ride again. UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: I literally had to force myself to not look at what I see and what everyone tells me, but to focus on what I believe in. UPSOUND: Dr Webster: I said I think it’s far too early to do it. And the next time he spoke to me was when he came back and said he’d done it. VO8: Eleven months after his accident, Grant returned to Italy and completed the Charly Gaul. UPSOUND: Glenn Lottering: The shoulder was so weak he couldn’t hold the handlebar. He was in so much pain. UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: It was still the hardest most painful ride I’ve ever done in my life, but also the most significant and most rewarding. VO9: The triumph whetted Grant’s appetite for the impossible. UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: I’ve done this with half a body literally. So I’m going to come back next year and I said to him I want to double. VO10: So the Im’Possible Tour was born, an annual solo ultra-endurance challenge. Driven by his brush with death, Grant invested his mission with a social purpose. UPSOUND: Morne du Plessis: Grant is quite obviously one of the bravest, determined people you would ever meet. He epitomises everything our organisation stands for. VO11: Morne du Plessis is chairperson of the Laureus Sport for Good Foundation which uses sports to drive social change. As an ambassador, Grant raises funds and awareness for its 26 local programmes. UPSOUND: Morne du Plessis: The funding is just one of the goals. The life lessons, the motivation, the inspiration that comes with this is as important. UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: I’m not on my own time anymore. This is a second chance at life I’ve been given. So I don’t want a day to go by that I waste it. LINK 3: Year after year, Grant returned to the mountains that almost took his life, pushing himself to the limits of endurance. VO12: In 2015, he was the first South African to complete a solo, non-stop, 420km ride through the French Alps in under 24 hours, climbing 10 000m. In 2016, he rode 962km in 46 hours, climbing 20,000m. UPSOUND: Glenn Lottering: Some of the routes, your cellphone doesn’t work, there’s no GPS, it’s tiny little roads. UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: I started hallucinating at times. I’d see hands in the bushes or a dog chasing me. Derek Watts: The battle’s with yourself really. Grant Lottering: Oh yeah. I know every demon [laughs] VO13: Following a cancer scare and more surgery, Grant set out in 2017 hoping to smash his own records. UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: I was going to ride 4 days, 1800km. UPSOUND: Glenn Lottering: What we weren’t prepared for was the temperatures that hit us that evening. The middle of the summer and suddenly we’re at minus 5, minus 10 degrees Celsius. UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: And by the next morning, I had ridden 400km, 20 hours and I already had hypothermia. VO14: Forced to give up, it was with even greater determination that Grant returned to those unforgiving mountains this year. UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: This is where I started, down in the Pyrenees near Spain. VO15: His route traversed the Pyrenees and the Alps, a total of 961km and over 21 000m of climbing in an ordeal lasting more than 72 hours. UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: Finished about an hour’s drive south of Geneva, Les Saisies. 23 mountains. Nineteen of the mountains I rode was in the Tour de France this year. UPSOUND: Glenn Lottering: Imagine you take 23 days of the Tour de France, or maybe let’s say 18, and you squeeze that into 2, 3 days. VO16: Grant faced road closures, getting lost in the middle of the night and rain that made the roads treacherous. He totalled less than 4 hours’ sleep. UPSOUND: Glenn Lottering: You come around a corner, he’s doing 80km an hour on a downhill and the sheep are lying in the road. When you get to the bottom you say a little prayer and you move on. VO17: It was a triumph of teamwork – and marked R2 million raised for Laureus. LINK 4: Well it’s Grant’s last European tour for now – but he has big plans to take on the South African landscape. UPSOUND: Grant: I want to ride across this country, five provinces. It’s going to be even harder than what I did this year. Derek Watts: Have you ever thought of table tennis? Very good sport. UPSOUND: Morne du Plessis: His story is about dedication and determination and getting up again. Sport with meaning. UPSOUND: Grant Lottering: Like anything in life, if you really put your mind to it and you commit and you persevere, you can accomplish some incredible things. PROMO 1: 10 SECONDS VO: After a near-fatal crash five years ago, Grant Lottering was told he’d never cycle again. But he turned defeat into triumph as an ultra-endurance athlete. Now his annual Im’Possible tour tests the limits of human endurance. This is a second chance at life I’ve been given. So I don’t want a day to go by that I waste it. VO: A cycling accident almost killed him five years ago, but Grant Lottering refused to accept defeat. Now his Im’Possible tour tests the limits of human endurance. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Grant Lottering has faced impossible odds on the bicycle - but he continues to push the boundaries of endurance.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: IN 2013 former professional cyclist Grant Lottering almost died on the side of the road in Italy after a dramatic crash during preparation for the world champs. He was told he would never get on a bike again but he swore from his hospital bed to complete the race in which he had crashed - the next year, he did. Since then, he has completed one solo ultra-endurance feat after another and proved the strength of the human spirit.
metadata.Summary: Grant Lottering was a professional cyclist who in July 2013 was training for the world champs in a 140km preparation race in Trento, Italy. Rounding a corner in the rain at 60km/h he crashed into a rock embankment, collapsing his lungs and thorax, crushing his shoulder, fracturing 12 ribs, his spine, femur, scapula, clavicle, and sternum, rupturing arteries…His heart had stopped beating by the time the medical team arrived. He was told he was lucky to be alive and would never ride a bike again. But even while he was still in hospital, he swore he would return the next year to complete the race in which he had crashed and one year later, after six surgeries and 83 rehabilitation sessions, he completed the ride 170km La Marmotte through the Alps, then the Charly Gaul – the race in which he almost died. Over the following four years he has tackled one endurance feat after another, riding hundreds of kilometres through the Alps under conditions that have ranged from tricky to treacherous. He has not always succeeded - in 2017 he was forced to give up due to freezing temperatures and howling wind - but he has proved the ability of the human spirit to triumph over impossible odds.
metadata.Further information: In 2015, Lottering did the second Im’Possible tour: he became the first South African to complete a solo, non-stop, 414km ultra-endurance ride through the French Alps in 24 hours. He cycled over eight alpine mountains and climbed 1 000m higher than Mount Everest in one day. He still had two metal pins in his right leg and hip, as well as a still-fractured right clavicle held in place with plates and screws. In 2016, Lottering completed his 3rd Im'possible tour: 962km in 46 hours of continuous riding, climbing 20,000m over 20 Alpine mountains and riding throughout the night twice. On 2 July 2017, Grant Lottering set out to tackle his 4th Im’possible Tour: 40 mountains, climbing 44 700m, over a distance of 1800km, in under 96 hours, non-stop. But below zero temperatures and a gale-force wind forced him to submit and he gave up after covering 406km and 9 mountains, a total elevation gain of 11 400m. In September 2018 he returned for his final tour: a gruelling traverse of the entire Pyrenees, from the Col d’Aubisque in the Western Pyrenees to the ski station of Les Saisies in the Northern Alps. He arrived at Les Saisies at 13:34 on 4 September, 72 hours and 34 minutes after setting out, having faced challenges from road closures forcing detours to getting lost in the middle of the night and cycling up the wrong mountains before having to make a U-turn, to rain that made the descents treacherous, dangerous and slow. Throughout the 72 hour ordeal, Lottering never slept, but ‘napped’ in the support car, totalling only three hours and 40 minutes of sleep in three days. To date, Lottering’s annual Im’possible Tours have raised over R2 million for this worthy organisation that fosters a love for sport in disadvantaged communities. He now works as a motivational speaker, using his story to inspire others to triumph against the odds.
